## Question

Can I update a Shiny app's data without redeploying the app?
This toy application will compare Zillow's estimated typical home values for
ten Northeast Ohio communities. The purpose is to learn a reusable workflow
through an app that is enjoyable to explore.

## Experiment

### The big picture

```text
Zillow city CSV
  -> publish-data.R: select, reshape, check
  -> board/: versioned pin + _pins.yaml manifest
  -> Quarto render, review, commit, push
  -> GitHub Pages: public read-only board
  -> shinyapps.io: Shiny reads the pin once per visitor session
```

Writing a local pin, publishing the website, and deploying the app are separate
actions. A fresh visitor session will read the published pin. An already-open
session will keep its snapshot; automatic polling is outside this first version.

**Status:** the data has been prepared and the local pin round-trip verified.
The public board is being published independently of this draft write-up.
The Shiny shell has no data controls or chart yet. Keep this page marked as a
draft until the learning exercise is ready to share.

### Files and packages

| Item | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `publish-data.R` | Manually prepare and write the data artifact |
| `board/` | Public pin files and their web manifest |
| `app/app.R` | Shiny UI and consumer logic; deployed independently |
| `index.qmd` | Learning record and eventual experiment write-up |

Work from the `ds_lab` root in Positron. Use the active R interpreter's installed
packages; do not introduce a new dependency environment for this small exercise.
We will use `readr`, `dplyr`, `tidyr`, `ggplot2`, `pins`, and `shiny` as needed.
Deployment will also need `rsconnect`. Check packages in the actual Positron R
session before installing anything.

### Completed step: download and inspect

Open `publish-data.R` and run its configuration assignments. Write one line
under section 1 to download `source_url` into an object named `housing_raw`.
The function to look up is `readr::read_csv()`.

Inspect three things:

1. `dim(housing_raw)`: how many regions and columns did we download?
2. `names(housing_raw)[1:12]`: which columns identify a place, and where do dates begin?
3. A few Ohio rows: how does Zillow identify Cleveland and its neighbors?

**Why this step:** the source is a nationwide wide table, with a column for each
month. Our pin will be a small local long table, with one row per community and
month. Inspecting the source makes that transformation understandable.

We reviewed the source, selected the ten communities, reshaped the monthly
columns, validated the result, and visually inspected a line plot. Writing
and reading the local RDS pin preserved the prepared object exactly.

### Next checkpoints

| Checkpoint | Evidence of success |
|---|---|
| Prepare | Ten Ohio communities, one row per community/month, a sensible local plot |
| Pin locally | `pin_read()` reproduces the prepared data; manifest lists the pin |
| Host | Rendered board files match the source board; public URL can be read with pins |
| Explore | Community selection and both chart views behave as intended |
| Update independently | A new app session reads a newly published pin without an app deployment |

The prepared dataset will have three columns: `community` (character), `date`
(Date), and `value` (numeric dollars). Pin metadata will record the source URL
and retrieval time. Dates in the data describe the observation period, which
is different from when we retrieved the file.

### App behavior we will build

Choose up to four of Cleveland, Lakewood, Rocky River, Westlake, Parma,
Cleveland Heights, Shaker Heights, Beachwood, Solon, and Strongsville. Start
with Cleveland, Lakewood, and Shaker Heights, and a starting year of 2015.

Use a single line chart with a dollar view and a percentage-change view.
The percentage baseline is the first month on or after the chosen start with
nonmissing values for all selected communities. Show the baseline date and
compute each community's change from its own value that month. If no common
month exists, show a helpful message. Zero selections or more than four also
produce a helpful message rather than a broken chart.

Keep missing values without filling them in, and show gaps rather than drawing
lines across missing months. Display the latest observation month, the source,
and the meaning of ZHVI. Do not silently substitute invented data on errors.

### Active step: publish the board

The web-hosted board needs both its version directories and `_pins.yaml`.
Call `pins::write_board_manifest()` after each pin write; the manifest is not
maintained automatically. See the [pins web-hosting guide](https://pins.rstudio.com/articles/using-board-url.html).

The root `_quarto.yml` explicitly copies `experiments/housing-pins/board/`
as a project resource, independently of this page's draft status. Verify that
every board file, including `_pins.yaml`, reaches
`docs/experiments/housing-pins/board/` unchanged. A source `.nojekyll` file is
also copied to `docs/` so GitHub Pages serves underscore-prefixed files.
The publisher makes the RDS files writable after writing the pin: pins marks
them read-only, which otherwise prevents Quarto replacing copied files on Windows.

Follow the root README's render/review/commit/push/verify procedure when ready
to publish. Publishing is an explicit step; running the publisher alone does
not update GitHub Pages. Do not remove `draft: true` until the write-up is ready.

The intended public board address is:
`https://mpfoley73.github.io/ds_lab/experiments/housing-pins/board/`.
After publication, verify `board_url()` and `pin_read()` against that address
before deploying only the `app/` directory to shinyapps.io.
Create the board and read the pin inside `server()` so each session checks the
published snapshot, rather than reading it only once at app process startup.

### Checks before calling this complete

- An unsuccessful download or missing/duplicate requested community stops the
  publisher before it writes a replacement pin.
- The long table has unique community/date keys and positive nonmissing values.
- The local pin round-trip preserves data types and missing observations.
- The rendered board's file names and bytes match the source board.
- Dollar and percentage charts work for one through four communities; the
  baseline is shared and percentage values start at zero.
- A temporary local copy with one missing observation demonstrates baseline
  selection and chart gaps. Do not publish the modified test copy.
- A second genuine data snapshot reaches a new app session without redeployment.
  If Zillow has no new data yet, leave this check pending rather than claiming it.

## Sources and limitations

[Zillow Research](https://www.zillow.com/research/data/) publishes the ZHVI data
used here. ZHVI estimates typical home values; it is not an individual appraisal
or the median price of homes sold that month. We chose the all-homes, mid-tier,
smoothed, seasonally adjusted city series.

Source availability, geography labels, and history can change. Historical
estimates can be revised. This proof of concept keeps those limitations visible
without adding a database, scheduler, map, forecasts, or a recovery framework.
